notes:
I've put together verse-by-verse notes on Exodus 18, using only what the pages I read actually say. **What's missing:** I didn't find anything on bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, catholic.com, oca.org, or the Lutheran and Pentecostal denominational sites, so the scholarly and Catholic notes are thin and there are no Orthodox notes. I also found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter. On the main split between traditions (v. 11), the views are those of individual commentators, not official church positions.

---

**Whole chapter: when did the visit happen?**
- Some say the visit is told out of time order. Poole thinks Jethro came after the Law was given at Sinai, because Israel is already camped at "the mount of God." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/18-5.htm
- Gill reports a Jewish disagreement. Saadiah Gaon put the visit before the Law was given. Aben Ezra put it in the second year, after the Tabernacle was set up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/18-5.htm
- Clarke (a Methodist) argues for a later date. Moses talks about God's statutes as already given (v. 16), and the burnt offerings look like the ones the Law later commands. https://studylight.org/commentaries/acc/exodus-18.html
- Keil disagrees. He says the judges could easily have been chosen within two days, since the people were all in one camp. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/18-1.htm
- Clarke also suggests why the story sits here. After the curse on Amalek in chapter 17, it shows that Jethro's people were not under that curse, even though they lived among the Amalekites. https://studylight.org/commentaries/acc/exodus-18.html
- Coffman sees two attitudes side by side: Amalek attacks Israel, Jethro befriends it. Both peoples were related to Abraham, and he says they picture the two ways the non-Jewish world would respond to God's kingdom. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/exodus-18.html

**v. 1**
- Guzik: Jethro was probably descended from Midian, Abraham's son by Keturah. That gives good reason to think he was a true priest of the true God. Guzik also cites a view that the Hebrew word could mean "brother-in-law." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/
- Barnes also thinks Jethro was probably Moses' brother-in-law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/18-1.htm
- Ellicott: the key thing Jethro heard was that the LORD had brought Israel out, and that is what made him set out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/18-1.htm
- Gill: Midian was close to Egypt, so the news would have spread there. Moses may also have sent messengers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/18-1.htm
- Precept Austin: Jethro gives the credit for the escape to the LORD, not to his son-in-law. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-18-commentary

**vv. 2–4**
- Benson: Moses probably sent his family back after the incident at the inn, when Zipporah's reluctance to circumcise their son nearly cost him his life (Exod. 4:25). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/18-1.htm
- Precept Austin offers another reason: the dangers Moses faced in leading the people out of Egypt. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-18-commentary
- Coffman cites a Jewish writer who says "sent back" really means "sent to her father's home." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/exodus-18.html
- Matthew Henry: Moses needed his family with him so that he could set an example of running a household well while leading God's people (1 Tim. 3:5). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/18-1.htm
- v. 4 – Guzik, quoting Cole: this is the only time Moses' second son is mentioned. The name Eliezer suggests his faith had revived, compared with the despair in the name Gershom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/

**v. 5**
- The Geneva Bible notes say Horeb is called "the mount of God" because God did many miracles there. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/18-5.htm
- Gill links the name to God appearing to Moses there at the burning bush. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/18-5.htm

**v. 6**
- The Pulpit Commentary agrees with Keil, Poole and others that Jethro sent a messenger ahead to speak for him. That explains why he seems to speak to Moses before Moses goes out to meet him. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-18.html
- Guzik suggests Moses may have learned more about real leadership from the shepherd-priest Jethro than from his Egyptian education. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/

**v. 7**
- Guzik: by bowing and kissing him, Moses honoured Jethro both as father-in-law and as a genuine priest. His high position did not make him proud. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/
- The Pulpit Commentary: Jethro shows no jealousy that his former shepherd now leads a nation, and Moses shows no arrogance. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-18.html

**v. 8**
- Guzik: Moses gave an honest report, telling of the hardships as well as the rescues. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/
- Matthew Henry: this full account was one of the things Jethro came for. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_018.cfm

**v. 9**
- Matthew Henry: Jethro, an onlooker, was more moved by God's kindness than many who actually received it. Henry adds that this was not the only time Gentile faith put Israel's unbelief to shame (Matt. 8:10). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/18-12.htm and https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_018.cfm
- Coffman rejects the reading that Jethro was grieved at Egypt's destruction. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/exodus-18.html

**v. 10**
- Clarke: Jethro first thanks God for saving Moses, then for freeing the people. https://studylight.org/commentaries/acc/exodus-18.html
- The Pulpit Commentary: "you" means everyone in the tent with Moses, not Moses and Aaron (Kalisch's view), because Aaron only arrives later. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-18.html

**v. 11: where commentators really differ. Was Jethro converted here, or already a believer?**
- **Already a believer: Clarke (Methodist).** Jethro probably already held the true faith of the patriarchs, since Moses would hardly have married into a pagan family. https://studylight.org/commentaries/acc/exodus-18.html
- **A new and clearer faith: Calvin (Reformed).** Calvin doesn't think Jethro had sacrificed to idols. But he worshipped "an unknown God" with a confused faith, so v. 12 seems to be his first sincere, legitimate sacrifice. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/18-12.html
- **A turn from many gods: Pulpit Commentary.** Like most non-Israelites, Jethro seems to have believed in many gods, and he now gives that up. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-18.html
- **Firstfruits of the nations: Keil.** In Jethro the first of the Gentiles entered fellowship with God's people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/18-1.htm
- **Weighing both views: Coffman.** He lays out both and cites writers who see a real conversion here. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/exodus-18.html
- **A middle position: Guzik.** Jethro may have known this truth before, but God's victory over Egypt's gods made it clearer. Quoting Cole, this may not be strict monotheism, but it leads to worshipping one God only. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/
- The Jamieson-Fausset-Brown commentary: Jethro saw that the contest was really against Egypt's idols, and that it showed they were nothing. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/exodus-18.html
- The Catholic Douay version renders the end of the verse as "An ill day for the Egyptians when they wronged you!" https://www.newadvent.org/bible/exo018.htm

**v. 12**
- Ellicott: Jethro held a priesthood like Melchizedek's. Just as Abraham accepted Melchizedek, Moses and Aaron accepted Jethro's priesthood by sharing the sacrificial meal. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/18-12.htm
- Barnes: the verse plainly shows Jethro was recognised as a priest of the true God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/18-12.html
- Wesley (in the Benson notes) and Matthew Henry: Jethro probably offered the sacrifice himself, because Israel's priesthood was not yet set up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/18-12.htm
- Henry notes that Jethro, not Aaron, is the one said to bring the offerings. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_018.cfm
- Calvin: the offering was properly made, since Moses, Aaron and the elders openly took part. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/18-12.html
- Henry draws a picture of Christ: Jethro, a Gentile, was as welcome at the meal as any Israelite, just as Gentiles are welcome to Christ, the bread of life. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_018.cfm
- Henry also notes that worshipping together makes friendship holy. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/18-12.htm
- **Modern scholarship.** The 1901 Jewish Encyclopedia's critical section reads this passage as Jethro introducing Moses and Aaron to the worship of Yahweh. Several scholars (Ghillany, Tiele, Stade, Budde and others) concluded that Yahweh was originally a god of the Kenites, and that Israel took up his worship through Moses. https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/tje/e/kenites.html
- Writers Coffman cites see a conversion in this passage, which they say undercuts that theory. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/exodus-18.html
- **Catholic.** The Catholic Encyclopedia says the meeting ended in an alliance with Midian. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/10596a.htm

**v. 13**
- Matthew Henry: even with a guest in the camp, Moses kept court all day. Necessary work comes before social courtesies. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_018.cfm
- Guzik, quoting Cole: "sat" and "stood" are technical legal terms for judge and litigant. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/
- Precept Austin links this to Exodus 17. Moses had not yet learned from Aaron and Hur holding up his hands, and was "holding up his hands by himself" all day. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-18-commentary

**v. 14**
- The Pulpit Commentary rejects the idea that Jethro objected to Moses sitting while the people stood. What he objected to was Moses judging everyone alone. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-18.html

**vv. 15–16**
- Precept Austin: the fact that people came "to inquire of God" shows they now respected Moses as their representative before God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-18-commentary
- Ellicott: the people wanted rulings they felt carried God's authority, and would not trust lower judges as much. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/18-1.htm
- Guzik: Moses could judge fairly because he knew God's word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/

**vv. 17–18**
- Guzik: the problem was not that Moses was unfit or uncaring. The job was simply too big, and justice was being delayed. He compares Acts 6:2–4. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: the system was not good for Moses, for justice, or for the people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/exodus-18.html

**v. 19**
- Clarke: Jethro's advice was probably inspired by God. https://studylight.org/commentaries/acc/exodus-18.html
- Precept Austin: "listen to me" is a firm command. Here Moses begins to be shown as a mediator who pleads with God for the people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-18-commentary
- Guzik: Moses' first duty was to pray for the people. He quotes Spurgeon (Baptist) comparing the Christian pastor to Moses, who must both teach the people and plead for them with God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/

**v. 20**
- Guzik: if the people knew God's word themselves, many disputes would be settled at once. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/
- The Pulpit Commentary: Moses keeps the job of teaching principles, while applying them to cases can be handed to others. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-18.html

**v. 21**
- Guzik lists four qualities: ability, godliness, truthfulness and honesty. He links this to 2 Tim. 2:2. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/
- The Pulpit Commentary: Jethro's stress on these qualities shows his own true piety. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/exodus-18.html
- Precept Austin estimates the plan would mean about 200,000 judges at the lowest level. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-18-commentary

**v. 22**
- Guzik: Moses still oversaw the hard cases. Delegating is a way of leading, not giving up leadership. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/
- Coffman: the plan did not weaken Moses' authority. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/exodus-18.html

**v. 23**
- Guzik: Jethro knew his advice came from outside Israel, so he told Moses to make sure God commanded it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/
- Matthew Henry: Jethro pointed Moses to a better counsellor than himself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_018.cfm
- Coffman: "their place" is usually taken to mean Canaan, which shows Jethro knew God's promises to the patriarchs. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/exodus-18.html
- Guzik: the people would be better served, since "justice delayed is justice denied." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/

**v. 24**
- Guzik, quoting Morgan: God taught Moses through an outsider. All human advice should be taken back to God for approval. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/
- Ellicott: the judges were not actually appointed until after the Law was given. https://biblehub.com/exodus/18-24.htm

**vv. 25–26**
- Precept Austin: Moses carried out the plan without adding to it or taking from it. Jethro is the ideal adviser, because he had no plan to stay and run things. https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-18-commentary
- Guzik: God valued the leaders of tens as much as the leaders of thousands. The plan was good for Moses, for the leaders and for the people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-18/
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown notes that a similar layered system of sheikhs still existed among the Towara Bedouin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/exodus-18.html

**v. 27**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the phrase means Moses "sent him away." That shows Jethro is not the Hobab whom Moses later begged to stay. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/18-27.html
- Matthew Henry: Jethro's descendants, the Kenites, were later spared because of this kindness (1 Sam. 15:6). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Exd/Exd_018.cfm
- Gotquestions also identifies Jethro as a Kenite, based on Judges 1:16. https://www.gotquestions.org/Kenites.html
